/Through Tuesday/...
Issued at 1236 PM MDT Tue Aug 25 2026

Satellite imagery shows cumulus clouds forming in the high country 
and radar shows the first showers of the day starting over the last 
hour or so in the high country. West to northwest flow aloft will 
continue for the next few days around the periphery of the high 
pressure currently situated over New Mexico. At the surface, upslope 
flow is expected for each of the next two afternoons. As we saw 
yesterday, this has brought the return of scattered rain chances to 
the area. Notably, temperatures are expected to "cool" into the 
upper 80s with the increase in cloud cover each afternoon. Have 
slightly nudged down high temperatures this afternoon for the Urban 
Corridor given the cloud cover sticking around and temperatures 
still in the low 70s at the present time. According to ACARS 
soundings, a cap remains in place as of 12pm given the limited 
heating this morning.

Showers and thunderstorms will continue to form in the high country 
early this afternoon before sliding into the I-25 Corridor by mid 
afternoon, initially favoring areas near the Palmer Divide and 
Cheyenne Ridge. The storms will then spread into the eastern plains 
by the late afternoon. DCAPE this afternoon will be around 1200-1400 
J/kg, which could translate to 40 to 50 mph wind gusts near any 
storm/outflow boundaries. These storms should gradually strengthen 
as they move into a more favorable environment in our eastern 
plains. 0-6 km bulk shear could briefly reach 30 kts and MLCAPE will 
approach 1000 J/kg in the far eastern plains. Strong winds and large 
hail are the main threats with these storms mainly east of a line 
from Sterling to Akron to Limon as storms start to cluster. We can't 
rule out a marginally severe storm between the I-25 corridor and the 
aforementioned locations this afternoon. With fast storm motion (~20 
kts) and only scattered storms today, only concerned with very 
isolated pockets of flooding.

Overnight tonight, outflow from storms to our east should move 
through and increase the low-level moisture for the eastern Plains. 
This could introduce a stratus deck tomorrow morning for the Urban 
Corridor and adjacent plains and potentially limit the overall 
severe potential. A weak disturbance is expected to slide through 
overhead for Northeast CO tomorrow afternoon and slightly increase 
storm coverage as well as increase the flow aloft. Frankly, there is 
currently a wide spread in solutions for tomorrow afternoon's 
environment for the Urban Corridor. Given the uncertainty, have 
slightly nudged down PoPs for the Urban Corridor to ~40%. Confidence 
increases as you move further east that a more favorable environment 
for severe storms will be in place. Nevertheless, MLCAPE could reach 
as high as 1500 to 2000 J/kg and 0-6 km bulk shear will be ~30-40 
kts for much of the plains for tomorrow afternoon. There is a slight 
(2/5) risk in place from the Storm Prediction Center for tomorrow 
afternoon for the I-25 corridor and adjacent plains. Strong winds 
and large hail of at least 1.5 inches in diameter will be the main 
threats. Storm timing will be similar to today with storms clearing 
our eastern plains counties by 8pm to 10pm. Although PWATs should be 
around 150-175% of normal, with fast storm motion (~25 kts) once 
again, am only concerned with isolated flooding for tomorrow at this 
time.

By Thursday, the high pressure is forecast to expand near the Four 
Corners, lowering rain chances. By Friday, rain chances are expected 
to be nearly shut off (except for an isolated chance in the high 
country). Subsequently the mid-level thermal ridge will strengthen 
and lead to highs in the mid-90s for the plains on Friday and 
Saturday. For Sunday and Monday, a shortwave trough is expected to 
move through the far northern US- along the Canada/US border- and 
shunt the high pressure off to the south and east. This should 
reintroduce more cloud cover and rain chances for the area, 
especially by Monday, with high temperatures lowering once again 
into the mid to upper 80s for the plains.
